## Observations

1. Swapping equal characters has no effect. Every useful swap moves one `1` by one position without changing the left-to-right order of the `1`s.
2. If the `k` ones start at positions \(p_1<\cdots<p_k\), the minimum cost to place them at specified positions \(q_1<\cdots<q_k\) is \(\sum_{i=1}^{k}|p_i-q_i|\).
3. A contiguous block starting at \(l\) has \(q_i=l+i-1\), so its cost is the sum of distances from \(l\) to the adjusted positions \(a_i=p_i-i+1\). These adjusted positions are already nondecreasing and all lie in the valid range \(1\) through \(N-k+1\).
4. A median minimizes the sum of absolute distances. If there are two middle values, either one gives the same minimum.

## Solution sketch

1. > Swapping equal characters has no effect. Every useful swap moves one `1` by one position without changing the left-to-right order of the `1`s.

   Read \(N\) and \(S\), then scan the string from left to right using one-based positions. Record each `1` position \(p_i\) in encounter order. That order determines which `1` goes to each position in the final block.

2. > If the `k` ones start at positions \(p_1<\cdots<p_k\), the minimum cost to place them at specified positions \(q_1<\cdots<q_k\) is \(\sum_{i=1}^{k}|p_i-q_i|\).

   Each `1` must move at least its distance to its target. To see that this lower bound is attainable, first move the left-moving ones to their targets in left-to-right order. Every earlier `1` is already left of the current target: it either reached its own target or started at or before its own target. Then move the right-moving ones in right-to-left order, so every later `1` is already at its target. In both passes the needed path is clear of other ones. Use the distance sum directly rather than simulating these swaps.

3. > A contiguous block starting at \(l\) has \(q_i=l+i-1\), so its cost is the sum of distances from \(l\) to the adjusted positions \(a_i=p_i-i+1\). These adjusted positions are already nondecreasing and all lie in the valid range \(1\) through \(N-k+1\).

   Convert each recorded position to \(a_i\). This subtracts the offset that the corresponding `1` must have inside the block, reducing the problem to choosing a single block start. No sorting or boundary correction is needed.

4. > A median minimizes the sum of absolute distances. If there are two middle values, either one gives the same minimum.

   Take a middle entry \(m\) of the adjusted list and print \(\sum_{i=1}^{k}|a_i-m|\). The list is guaranteed to be nonempty. With one `1`, or when the ones are already contiguous, all adjusted positions are equal and the result is zero. The algorithm takes \(O(N)\) time and \(O(k)\) auxiliary space beyond the input string.
